entities.name: Isidore of Kyiv
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Isidore of Kyiv (c. 1385 – 1463), also known as Isidore of Thessalonica, was a prominent Byzantine Greek cardinal and theologian, whose life encapsulated the tumultuous 15th-century attempts to bridge the Great Schism between the Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches. Appointed Metropolitan of Kyiv and all Rus' in 1437 by Patriarch Joseph II of Constantinople, Isidore became a pivotal figure in the Council of Florence, championing the short-lived Union of Florence (1439) with an unwavering commitment to Christian unity. His career spanned significant ecclesiastical and political challenges, from his efforts to implement the union in Orthodox lands to his later role as a papal legate and cardinal.

His most defining contribution occurred at the Council of Florence (1438-1439), where, as a key representative of the Eastern Church, he ardently advocated for reconciliation. Isidore was one of the signatories of the *Laetentur Caeli*, the bull proclaiming the union, on July 6, 1439. Upon his return to Moscow in 1441 to promulgate the union, he was met with fierce resistance from Prince Vasili II and the local clergy, who rejected the council's decrees. Arrested and imprisoned, Isidore eventually escaped, making his way to Rome in 1443, where he was elevated to cardinal by Pope Eugenius IV, solidifying his allegiance to the Latin Church.

Isidore's strenuous efforts for church unity ultimately failed to take root in Muscovy, leading to the de facto autocephaly of the Russian Orthodox Church and its increased independence from Constantinople. His commitment, however, continued through his service as a papal legate, notably in Constantinople during its final siege in 1453, where he valiantly participated in its defense against the Ottoman Turks. After the city's fall, he continued to play a significant role within the Roman Curia, engaging in diplomatic missions and advocating for crusades against the Ottomans until his death in Rome in 1463.
